is completed before the first (in the stomach), which is called <term>chylification</term> <gloss>the process of turning food into chyle</gloss>. The excrements of the first and second <term>coction</term> <gloss>digestion/cooking</gloss> (namely in the intestines, and in the vessels of urine and bile) are contemporary with the digestive organs themselves. Finally, not only in the vegetative part of the soul, but even before the soul itself, there resides mind, providence, and intellect, which immediately from the first origin arrange, order, and provide for all things for the being and well-being of the chick, and fashion them with art into the form and likeness of their progenitors.

Concerning this likeness of the offspring, it is permissible to doubt what the reason might be why the fetus is sometimes found to be more similar to the father, sometimes to the mother, and sometimes even to grandparents, whether on the paternal or maternal side, especially when multiple eggs are fertilized in a single mating and at the same moment. It is also admirable that virtues and vices, as well as diseases, marks, and birthmarks, are transferred from parents to offspring, and this only in some fetuses, but not in all. In the chicken species, some are noble and born for battle; they prefer to die rather than yield to adversaries by fleeing. Yet their descendants, unless they were born of similar parents, gradually lose that virtue, according to the saying: the brave are created from the brave. In most other species of animals (and especially in humans), the nobility of the lineage is observed, and many gifts of mind and body arrive through descent.

I have often wondered why, since we see the offspring obtain (for the most part) a certain mixed structure or composition from both parents, and this in all other parts, the same does not happen in the genitals, but generally either a male or a female is born, and very rarely a hermaphrodite.

Finally, many things are present before they appear, and certain things are begun among the first that are perfected last, such as the eyes, the genitals, and the beak.
